confidence_note: The old text's Grove quote ('if you don't know where you're going...'), its claim that Doerr joined Intel in 1975 as a young engineer, and 'Google uses OKRs every quarter to this day' are not tied to the book and are dropped; sources say Doerr joined Intel in 1974 as a salesman, but the year is not used. Used instead: Operation Crush at Intel, told on whatmatters.com (Doerr's own site) and in Intel and Computer History Museum pages: late 1979 telex from district sales manager Don Buckout, forwarded by Casey Powell to Andy Grove; objective 'Establish the 8086 as the highest performance 16-bit microprocessor family'; target of 2,000 design wins; Crush teams to field offices in January 1980 with Grove videos; Motorola beaten by end of 1980; the 8088 later powered the first IBM PC. Final design-win count differs between sources (about 2,300 to almost 2,500) so it is left out. Doerr's role in the story was not confirmed as a participant.
facts: In late November 1979 Intel's 8086 chip was losing ground to Motorola's 68000.
A district sales manager, Don Buckout, sent headquarters an eight-page telex about it.
His boss Casey Powell forwarded it to Andy Grove, then Intel's president and COO.
The executive staff met within a week and a task force formed the week after.
The objective was written as: Establish the 8086 as the highest performance 16-bit microprocessor family.
The target was 2,000 design wins, meaning customers agreeing to build the chip into their products.
In January 1980 Crush teams went to field offices worldwide, supported by videos of Grove.
Intel changed no product for the campaign; it changed how it sold, aiming at long-term systems and service.
By the end of 1980 Intel had beaten Motorola, and the 8088 later powered the first IBM PC.
The 8086 was Intel's first high-performance 16-bit microprocessor; the task force judged Zilog a minor threat and Motorola the real danger.
By the second quarter of 1980 the sales organization had deployed the new approach; by 1986 the 8086 had regained 85% of the 16-bit market.
scene_details: videos of Grove sent to field offices
tension: An eight-page telex from a district sales manager reached the president within days.
opening_idea: Start with the eight-page telex that Don Buckout sent in November 1979.

lessons.idea: A goal written as an objective plus a countable target lets a whole organization move in the same direction.
lessons.anchor: One sentence of objective and 2,000 design wins.

reflect_final: What is one thing you are working on now that has a clear objective but no number that would tell you it was reached?

use_cases.situation: A project has a vague aim.
use_cases.move: Write the objective in one sentence and one number that shows it was reached, as Intel did with 2,000 design wins.

use_cases.situation: Your team lead asks what you will focus on.
use_cases.move: Say the objective and the one number you will check at the end of the quarter.

use_cases.situation: You want to start a personal goal.
use_cases.move: Write the sentence and the countable target on one page.

pocket_idea: Intel wrote one objective and one number, 2,000 design wins: write your own sentence and number.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: A district manager's eight-page telex became Intel's Operation Crush within a few weeks.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: In late 1979 Intel's 8086 was losing to Motorola. District sales manager Don Buckout sent an eight-page telex, it reached Andy Grove, and the company set one objective and a target of 2,000 design wins. Crush teams went to field offices in January 1980, and by year's end Intel had beaten Motorola. The chip later powered the first IBM PC.
